definition: Measuring the amplitude of a continuous-time signal at discrete instants of time.
wrongs: Mapping each measured amplitude onto the nearest level from a finite set.
Shifting a message onto a high-frequency carrier for radio transmission.
Sharing one link among several signals by frequency or time.
why: Sampling keeps the amplitude at chosen instants and discards the waveform between those instants.
example: A 4 kHz voice waveform is measured 8000 times each second and stored as a sequence of amplitudes.
scenario: A thermometer voltage is read every 1 ms and the values between those instants are not kept. Which operation is this?
scenarioWhy: Reading a continuous signal at discrete instants is sampling.

definition: The result that a band-limited signal can be reconstructed from samples taken at least twice its highest frequency.
wrongs: The claim that any signal can be reconstructed from one sample per minute.
The rule that a noisy channel's capacity equals bandwidth times the SNR in decibels.
The statement that parity bits can correct every burst of errors.
why: If sampling is at least twice the highest frequency, the original band-limited signal is determined by its samples.
example: A recording whose highest frequency is 5 kHz is kept reconstructable by sampling at 10 kHz or faster.
scenario: The highest frequency in a recording is 5 kHz. Which minimum sampling rate does the sampling theorem require?
scenarioWhy: The theorem requires a sampling rate of at least twice 5 kHz, which is 10 kHz.

definition: The minimum sampling frequency for a band-limited signal, equal to twice its highest frequency.
wrongs: Half the sampling frequency, which is the highest frequency the samples can represent.
The maximum bit rate of a noisy channel from Shannon's formula.
The symbol rate multiplied by the carrier frequency.
why: Sampling slower than twice the highest frequency is not sufficient for reconstruction, so that product is the minimum rate.
example: A sensor signal band-limited to 3.4 kHz has a Nyquist rate of 6.8 kHz.
scenario: A baseband signal contains no energy above 3.4 kHz. Which sampling frequency is its Nyquist rate?
scenarioWhy: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency, so 2 times 3.4 kHz is 6.8 kHz.

definition: Half the sampling frequency, above which components fold back into lower frequencies.
wrongs: Twice the highest frequency in the original signal, which is the minimum sampling rate.
The carrier frequency used for passband transmission.
The bandwidth of a raised-cosine filter's excess spectrum.
why: Frequencies above half the sampling rate cannot be represented uniquely and alias about that folding frequency.
example: An 8 kHz sampler has a folding frequency of 4 kHz, so a 5 kHz tone will not stay at 5 kHz.
scenario: Samples are taken at 8000 samples per second. Which frequency is the folding frequency?
scenarioWhy: The folding frequency is half the sampling frequency, and half of 8 kHz is 4 kHz.

definition: The effect in which frequencies above half the sampling rate appear as lower frequencies in the samples.
wrongs: The loss of signal power as a wave travels down a cable.
Overlap of pulse energy into neighboring symbol intervals.
A remainder left after polynomial division of a frame.
why: Under-sampling folds high frequencies about half the sampling rate, so they masquerade as lower frequencies.
example: A 6 kHz tone sampled at 8 kHz shows up in the samples as a 2 kHz tone.
scenario: A 6 kHz sine wave is sampled at 8 kHz with no anti-alias filter. Which frequency appears in the sample sequence?
scenarioWhy: The tone folds about 4 kHz, and the distance from 6 kHz to 8 kHz is 2 kHz.

definition: Mapping each sample's amplitude to one of a finite set of discrete levels.
wrongs: Measuring a continuous waveform at evenly spaced instants.
Adding a parity bit so the number of 1s is even.
Assigning each user a separate frequency band.
why: After sampling, quantization replaces a continuous amplitude with the nearest allowed representation level.
example: Each temperature sample is forced to the nearest of 256 evenly spaced voltage levels.
scenario: Every sample of a speech waveform is replaced by the nearest of 256 allowed amplitudes. Which step is that?
scenarioWhy: Choosing one of a finite set of amplitudes for each sample is quantization.

definition: The difference between a sample's true amplitude and the discrete level chosen for it.
wrongs: The gap in time between two successive sampling instants.
The number of bits used to number a PCM code word.
The delay of a symbol through a band-limited channel.
why: The level is only an approximation, so the original amplitude and the chosen level differ by the quantization error.
example: A 1.37 V sample is stored as the 1.25 V level, leaving a 0.12 V error.
scenario: A sample is 1.37 V and the nearest reconstruction level is 1.25 V. Which value is the magnitude of the quantization error?
scenarioWhy: The error magnitude is the absolute difference, 1.37 minus 1.25, which is 0.12 V.

definition: A method that samples a signal, quantizes each sample, and encodes the levels as binary code words.
wrongs: A one-bit scheme that sends only the sign of each step from a staircase approximation.
A passband method that switches a carrier among four phases.
A check value formed as a polynomial remainder.
why: Pulse code modulation is the chain of sampling, quantization, and binary encoding of the quantized levels.
example: Telephone voice is sampled 8000 times a second and each sample is sent as an 8-bit code word.
scenario: A voice line is sampled, each sample is assigned a level, and each level is transmitted as 8 bits. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: Sampling, quantizing, and binary encoding together are pulse code modulation.

definition: Compressing a signal's amplitude range before uniform quantization and expanding it at the receiver.
wrongs: Sending only one bit that says whether to step the approximation up or down.
Dividing the data polynomial by a generator to form a frame check.
Giving each caller a fixed repeating time slot.
why: Compression gives small signals more of the quantizer's resolution, and expansion restores the original range.
example: A mu-law codec boosts quiet speech before an 8-bit uniform quantizer and restores it after decoding.
scenario: Quiet speech is stretched before a uniform quantizer and compressed back after decoding. Which technique is this?
scenarioWhy: Compressing before quantization and expanding afterward is companding.

definition: A one-bit scheme that transmits only whether the approximation should step up or down.
wrongs: Encoding each sample as a multi-bit code word after uniform quantization.
Changing both amplitude and phase so one symbol carries several bits.
Appending a checksum formed by adding 16-bit data words.
why: Each sample interval carries a single bit, the sign of the difference from the staircase approximation.
example: A modem sends a 1 to raise the staircase by one step and a 0 to lower it by one step.
scenario: The transmitter sends one bit per sample interval meaning step up or step down from the staircase. Which scheme is this?
scenarioWhy: A single up-or-down bit each interval is delta modulation.

definition: Encoding the difference between a sample and a predicted value, using more than a sign bit.
wrongs: Sending only the sign of a one-step staircase change.
Mapping bits to mid-bit voltage transitions for clock recovery.
Assigning each user the full bandwidth in a fixed time slot.
why: Differential PCM quantizes a prediction error, which is smaller than the sample and can use several bits.
example: A codec predicts the next speech sample and transmits a 4-bit code for the prediction error.
scenario: The encoder transmits a 4-bit code for the gap between a new sample and its prediction. Which scheme is this?
scenarioWhy: A multi-bit encoding of the prediction error is differential PCM, not one-bit delta modulation.

definition: Varying a property of a carrier wave, such as amplitude, frequency, or phase, in step with a message.
wrongs: Reading a baseband waveform at discrete time instants.
Replacing amplitudes with the nearest finite set of levels.
Detecting errors by recomputing a parity bit.
why: The message changes a chosen parameter of the carrier so the information can occupy a desired frequency band.
example: A microphone waveform changes the amplitude of a 100 kHz sinusoid before it is sent to an antenna.
scenario: A 100 kHz sinusoid has its amplitude varied so a microphone waveform can cross a radio channel. Which operation is applied to the sinusoid?
scenarioWhy: Changing a carrier parameter in step with a message is modulation.

definition: Digital modulation that represents symbols by discrete amplitudes of a carrier at one frequency.
wrongs: Digital modulation that switches a constant-amplitude carrier among discrete frequencies.
Digital modulation that keeps amplitude fixed and changes only the carrier phase.
A baseband line code that inserts a transition in the middle of every bit.
why: The information is carried in the carrier amplitude, while the carrier frequency stays the same.
example: A transmitter sends a full-strength 10 MHz tone for 1 and turns that tone off for 0.
scenario: Bits are sent on one frequency as either full carrier amplitude or zero amplitude. Which scheme is this?
scenarioWhy: Changing only the carrier amplitude to represent bits is amplitude shift keying.

definition: Digital modulation that represents symbols by switching a carrier among discrete frequencies.
wrongs: Digital modulation that uses one frequency and changes only the carrier amplitude.
Digital modulation that encodes symbols as points with both amplitude and phase.
A detection code computed as a polynomial remainder.
why: Each symbol selects a frequency, so the receiver distinguishes symbols by which tone arrived.
example: A modem sends 1200 Hz for binary 0 and 2200 Hz for binary 1 at constant amplitude.
scenario: A modem uses 1200 Hz for 0 and 2200 Hz for 1, with amplitude held constant. Which scheme is this?
scenarioWhy: Switching between discrete carrier frequencies is frequency shift keying.

definition: Digital modulation that represents symbols by discrete phases of a constant-amplitude carrier.
wrongs: Digital modulation that represents bits by turning the carrier amplitude on or off.
Digital modulation that assigns a different frequency to each symbol.
A line code that uses a mid-bit transition and no carrier.
why: The receiver recovers the symbol from the phase shift, while the carrier amplitude stays constant.
example: A transmitter uses 0 degrees for bit 0 and 180 degrees for bit 1 on a fixed-amplitude carrier.
scenario: Amplitude stays fixed, 0 degrees means bit 0, and 180 degrees means bit 1. Which scheme is this?
scenarioWhy: Encoding bits as discrete carrier phases is phase shift keying.

definition: Phase shift keying that uses four carrier phases so each symbol carries two bits.
wrongs: Binary phase shift keying that uses two phases and carries one bit per symbol.
Frequency shift keying that uses two tones and carries one bit per tone.
On-off keying that uses the presence or absence of a carrier.
why: Four phases give four symbols, and four symbols can represent two bits each.
example: A satellite link maps 00, 01, 11, and 10 onto four phases spaced 90 degrees apart.
scenario: A link uses four phases spaced 90 degrees apart, and each transmitted symbol stands for two bits. Which scheme is this?
scenarioWhy: Four phases carrying two bits per symbol is quadrature phase shift keying.

definition: Modulation that encodes symbols by changing both the amplitude and the phase of a carrier.
wrongs: Modulation that changes only the carrier frequency and keeps amplitude fixed.
Modulation that changes only the carrier phase and keeps amplitude fixed.
A baseband code that never uses a carrier.
why: Each symbol is a pair of amplitude and phase, plotted as a point in the in-phase and quadrature plane.
example: A cable modem uses 16 points, each with its own amplitude and phase, to send 4 bits per symbol.
scenario: A 16-point scheme changes both amplitude and phase so each symbol carries four bits. Which family is this?
scenarioWhy: Symbols that differ in both amplitude and phase belong to quadrature amplitude modulation.

definition: A plot of each symbol as a point in the in-phase and quadrature plane.
wrongs: A time-domain display of many overlaid traces used to judge eye opening.
A plot of gain versus frequency for a linear filter.
A chart of reflection coefficient on a radio-frequency transmission line.
why: The horizontal and vertical axes are the two carrier components, so each legal symbol is one point.
example: An engineer plots 16-QAM as a 4-by-4 grid of dots and watches noise clouds around each dot.
scenario: Received symbols are drawn as dots on the I and Q axes to see which decision region they fall in. Which display is this?
scenarioWhy: Symbol points in the I-Q plane form a constellation diagram.

definition: A high-frequency wave whose amplitude, frequency, or phase is varied to carry a message.
wrongs: The low-frequency message waveform before any frequency shift.
The extra parity bit appended to a data block.
The clock recovered from mid-bit transitions.
why: The carrier itself is a sinusoid chosen so the modulated signal occupies the channel's passband.
example: A Wi-Fi transmission uses a 2.4 GHz wave as the wave that is modulated by the data symbols.
scenario: The data are recovered from a 2.4 GHz wave that served only as the vehicle for the symbols. Which wave is the 2.4 GHz signal?
scenarioWhy: The high-frequency wave that is modulated by the message is the carrier.

definition: Sending a signal whose spectrum is concentrated near zero frequency, without a carrier shift.
wrongs: Sending information on a carrier so the spectrum is centered at a high frequency.
Combining many optical wavelengths on one fiber.
Correcting errors from redundant bits with no retransmission.
why: The pulses or the message spectrum stay around zero frequency instead of being moved to a carrier.
example: An Ethernet pair carries Manchester pulses whose energy is near zero frequency rather than on a radio carrier.
scenario: A copper link sends voltage pulses with the spectrum sitting near 0 Hz and no radio-frequency shift. Which form of transmission is this?
scenarioWhy: A spectrum concentrated near zero, with no carrier shift, is baseband transmission.

definition: Sending information by modulating it onto a carrier so the spectrum is centered away from zero.
wrongs: Sending pulses whose spectrum remains concentrated near zero frequency.
Sampling a waveform at twice its highest frequency.
Detecting a frame error with a single parity bit.
why: Modulation translates the message spectrum so it is centered on the carrier frequency.
example: A handset modulates data onto a 5 GHz carrier, and the transmitted spectrum sits around 5 GHz.
scenario: Wi-Fi shifts the data onto a 5 GHz carrier so the spectrum is centered on that carrier. Which form of transmission is this?
scenarioWhy: A spectrum centered on a high-frequency carrier is passband transmission.

definition: The number of symbols transmitted per second.
wrongs: The number of information bits transmitted per second in every modulation.
The highest frequency present in the original message.
The ratio of signal power to noise power.
why: Each symbol is one signaling interval, so the symbol rate is how many of those intervals occur each second.
example: A modem emits 2400 distinct symbols each second, regardless of how many bits each symbol holds.
scenario: A link emits 2000 symbols each second, and each symbol may represent more than one bit. Which quantity is 2000 per second?
scenarioWhy: Symbols per second is the symbol rate, even when a symbol holds several bits.

definition: The number of information bits transmitted per second.
wrongs: The number of symbols transmitted per second, ignoring bits per symbol.
The width of the channel in hertz.
The fraction of received bits that are wrong.
why: Bit rate multiplies the symbol rate by the number of information bits carried in each symbol.
example: QPSK at 1000 symbols per second delivers 2000 information bits per second.
scenario: QPSK sends 1000 symbols per second. Which information bit rate results?
scenarioWhy: QPSK carries two bits per symbol, so 1000 symbols per second is 2000 bit/s.

definition: Unwanted random energy added to a signal that can cause the receiver to decide incorrectly.
wrongs: The intended message waveform before it is modulated.
A planned reduction of bandwidth by an ideal low-pass filter.
The useful carrier that transports the symbols.
why: Noise is not part of the transmitted message; it disturbs the received waveform and can flip decisions.
example: Thermal agitation in a receiver front end adds a random voltage to a weak incoming radio signal.
scenario: A random electrical disturbance on the cable flips a receiver's bit decision. Which impairment is that disturbance?
scenarioWhy: Unwanted random energy that corrupts decisions is noise.

definition: A channel model that adds noise with a Gaussian amplitude distribution and a flat spectrum.
wrongs: A noiseless channel whose bit rate is only 2B log2 of the number of levels.
A code that corrects errors by polynomial division.
A frame format that assigns fixed time slots.
why: The noise is additive, its samples are Gaussian, and white means its power spectral density is constant.
example: A link budget models the receiver as the signal plus Gaussian noise whose spectrum is flat across the band.
scenario: The design adds noise that is Gaussian, spectrally flat, and simply summed with the signal. Which model is this?
scenarioWhy: Additive, white, and Gaussian noise is the AWGN model.

definition: The ratio of average signal power to average noise power.
wrongs: The difference in hertz between the highest and lowest passed frequencies.
The number of symbols sent per second.
The fraction of bits received in error.
why: Comparing signal power with noise power, often as 10 log10 of that ratio in decibels, gives the SNR.
example: A receiver measures signal power 100 times the noise power and reports an SNR of 20 dB.
scenario: Signal power is 100 times the noise power. Which SNR in decibels is that?
scenarioWhy: Ten times the base-10 log of 100 is 20, so the SNR is 20 dB.

definition: The width of the frequency band a signal occupies or a channel passes, measured in hertz.
wrongs: The ratio of signal power to noise power in decibels.
The number of bits transmitted each second.
The time delay from the first bit leaving the sender to its arrival.
why: Bandwidth is an interval of frequency, the highest passed frequency minus the lowest, not a bit rate.
example: A voice channel that passes 300 Hz through 3300 Hz has a bandwidth of 3000 Hz.
scenario: A channel passes 300 Hz through 3300 Hz and rejects everything else. Which bandwidth does it have?
scenarioWhy: Bandwidth is the difference of the band edges, 3300 minus 300, which is 3000 Hz.

definition: The theoretical maximum error-free bit rate of a noisy channel, bandwidth times log2 of one plus the SNR.
wrongs: The noiseless limit of twice the bandwidth times log2 of the number of levels.
The minimum sampling rate of twice the highest message frequency.
The Hamming distance between two particular codewords.
why: Shannon's formula uses bandwidth and the linear signal-to-noise ratio to bound reliable communication.
example: A 3 kHz channel with SNR power ratio 1023 has a Shannon capacity of 30 kbit/s.
scenario: Bandwidth is 3000 Hz and the SNR power ratio is 1023. Which capacity does Shannon's formula give?
scenarioWhy: Capacity is 3000 times log2 of 1024, and log2 of 1024 is 10, so the result is 30 kbit/s.

definition: The maximum bit rate of a noiseless channel, twice the bandwidth times log2 of the number of signal levels.
wrongs: The noisy-channel limit given by bandwidth times log2 of one plus the SNR.
The minimum sampling frequency of twice the highest message frequency.
Half the sampling frequency, called the folding frequency.
why: With no noise, a channel of bandwidth B can carry 2B symbols per second, and each symbol can hold log2(M) bits.
example: A noiseless 4000 Hz channel with two levels has a Nyquist bit rate of 8000 bit/s.
scenario: A noiseless channel has bandwidth 4000 Hz and 2 signal levels. Which maximum bit rate does the Nyquist formula give?
scenarioWhy: The noiseless rate is 2 times 4000 times log2 of 2, which is 8000 bit/s.

definition: The loss of signal power as the signal travels through a medium.
wrongs: The addition of Gaussian noise with a flat spectrum.
The folding of high frequencies into lower ones by slow sampling.
The overlap of one symbol's energy into the next symbol interval.
why: The medium absorbs or spreads energy, so received power is lower than transmitted power.
example: A coaxial run delivers only 1/100 of the transmitted power, a loss of 20 dB.
scenario: Received power is 1/100 of the transmitted power. Which attenuation in decibels is that?
scenarioWhy: Attenuation is 10 log10 of 100, which is 20 dB.

definition: The fraction of received bits that are decoded incorrectly.
wrongs: The number of information bits sent per second.
The ratio of signal power to noise power.
The number of symbols sent per second.
why: Bit error rate counts wrong bits and divides by the number of bits received in the same interval.
example: A test finds 8 wrong bits in 4000 received bits, so the bit error rate is 0.002.
scenario: Eight bits are wrong in 4000 received bits. Which bit error rate is that?
scenarioWhy: Eight errors divided by 4000 bits is 0.002.

definition: Using added redundancy to decide whether a received block contains errors, without necessarily repairing it.
wrongs: Repairing corrupted bits at the receiver from redundant checks, with no retransmission.
Modulating a carrier's phase to represent the data.
Sampling faster than the Nyquist rate to avoid aliasing.
why: Detection only flags a damaged block; correction or a retransmission request is a further step.
example: A receiver recomputes a frame check, finds it does not match, and discards the frame.
scenario: The receiver can tell a frame is damaged but cannot repair the bits, so it drops the frame. Which capability is it using?
scenarioWhy: Recognizing a damaged block without fixing the bits is error detection.

definition: An extra bit set so the count of 1s in a block is even or odd, used to notice bit errors.
wrongs: A start bit that only marks the beginning of an asynchronous character.
A stuffing bit inserted so a flag pattern does not appear in the data.
A sign bit that records whether a quantized sample is positive.
why: The sender chooses the extra bit to force the agreed parity, and the receiver checks that the parity still holds.
example: A 7-bit character gains one more bit so the whole 8-bit group has even parity before it is sent.
scenario: One extra bit is appended so a single flipped bit in the block can be noticed. Which added bit is this in the simplest scheme?
scenarioWhy: An extra bit that forces even or odd parity is a parity bit.

definition: A rule that sets the extra bit so the block, including that bit, contains an even number of 1s.
wrongs: A rule that sets the extra bit so the block contains an odd number of 1s.
A rule that always appends 1 regardless of the data.
A rule that repeats every data bit twice.
why: The parity bit is 0 when the data already has an even number of 1s, and 1 when it has an odd number.
example: Data 1011001 already has four 1s, so the even-parity bit appended to it is 0.
scenario: Data bits are 1011001, which contain four 1s. Which even-parity bit should be appended?
scenarioWhy: Four 1s is already even, so the even-parity bit is 0.

definition: A detection value formed by summing data words and appending that sum for the receiver to recompute.
wrongs: A remainder from dividing the data by a generator polynomial.
A set of overlapping parity bits that corrects a single-bit error.
A mid-bit transition used only for clock recovery.
why: The receiver adds the same words, including the appended sum, and a mismatch indicates a detected error.
example: A sender adds its 16-bit words, appends the sum, and the receiver rejects the packet when its sum differs.
scenario: The sender adds the 16-bit words and appends the sum; the receiver adds them again and compares. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: Detection by summing data words is a checksum, not polynomial division.

definition: A detection code formed as the remainder of dividing the data polynomial by a generator polynomial.
wrongs: A detection value formed by adding the data words in ordinary arithmetic.
A single extra bit that makes the number of 1s even.
A line code with a transition in the middle of each bit.
why: Polynomial division by the generator produces a remainder that is appended and recomputed at the receiver.
example: A frame check is the remainder after division by the generator x^16 + x^12 + x^5 + 1.
scenario: The frame check is the remainder after dividing the data by a generator polynomial. Which code is this?
scenarioWhy: A remainder from generator-polynomial division is a cyclic redundancy check.

definition: The number of bit positions in which two equal-length binary words differ.
wrongs: The smallest distance between any pair of codewords in a whole code.
The physical length of the cable between two modems.
The number of parity bits in a CRC generator.
why: Comparing the words position by position and counting mismatches gives their Hamming distance.
example: The words 10110 and 10011 differ in the third and fifth positions, so their distance is 2.
scenario: The words 10110 and 10011 differ in two bit positions. Which Hamming distance is that?
scenarioWhy: Two differing positions give a Hamming distance of 2.

definition: A binary block code that uses overlapping parity bits to correct any single-bit error.
wrongs: A detection-only remainder from polynomial division that does not locate a bit error.
A single parity bit that can notice an odd number of errors but cannot correct one.
A convolutional code whose parity depends on a sliding window of many input bits.
why: Parity checks at chosen positions form a syndrome that identifies which single bit to flip.
example: A (7,4) Hamming code sends 4 data bits and 3 parity bits and repairs one flipped bit.
scenario: A (7,4) code corrects one flipped bit using parity checks at power-of-two positions. Which code family is this?
scenarioWhy: Overlapping parity bits that correct one error identify a Hamming code.

definition: The smallest Hamming distance between any two different valid codewords of a code.
wrongs: The distance between one received word and one particular codeword.
The number of data bits in a codeword before parity is added.
The generator polynomial's degree.
why: Detection and correction limits are set by this smallest separation: it corrects t errors when the distance is at least 2t+1.
example: If the closest distinct codewords differ in 3 positions, the code's minimum distance is 3.
scenario: A code's closest distinct codewords differ in 3 positions, and no pair is closer. How many errors can the code correct?
scenarioWhy: A minimum distance of 3 satisfies 2t+1 = 3, so the code corrects t = 1 error.

definition: Correcting errors at the receiver from redundant bits, with no request for a retransmission.
wrongs: Detecting a bad block and asking the sender to transmit that block again.
Dropping every damaged frame and sending no repair and no request.
Compressing amplitudes before quantization.
why: The redundancy is enough for the receiver to reconstruct the message without a return channel.
example: A deep-space probe uses a correcting code because a retransmission would take too long.
scenario: A satellite link has a huge delay, so the receiver fixes single-bit errors locally and does not ask for a resend. Which strategy is this?
scenarioWhy: Local correction without a retransmission request is forward error correction.

definition: An error-control strategy that detects a bad block and asks the sender to transmit it again.
wrongs: Correcting the bad block locally from redundant bits and sending no request.
Modulating the block onto a higher-frequency carrier.
Multiplexing the block with other users by wavelength.
why: Automatic repeat request depends on detection plus a feedback path that triggers retransmission.
example: A data link discards a frame with a bad check and returns a negative acknowledgement so the frame is resent.
scenario: A bad frame is detected and the sender is told to transmit that frame again. Which strategy is this?
scenarioWhy: Asking for the damaged block to be sent again is automatic repeat request.

definition: Combining several independent signals so they share one communication link.
wrongs: Changing a carrier's amplitude to carry one message.
Sampling one waveform at twice its highest frequency.
Correcting one message with a Hamming code.
why: Multiplexing divides the link by frequency, time, wavelength, or code so more than one signal can use it.
example: Four phone calls share one trunk instead of four separate copper pairs.
scenario: Four independent calls share one trunk instead of four separate cables. Which general technique allows the sharing?
scenarioWhy: Combining independent signals onto one shared link is multiplexing.

definition: Multiplexing that gives each signal its own frequency band at the same time.
wrongs: Multiplexing that gives each signal the full bandwidth during its own time slot.
Multiplexing that separates users by orthogonal spreading codes.
Optical multiplexing that assigns each signal a wavelength on a fiber.
why: The signals occupy the link simultaneously, separated by non-overlapping frequency bands and often guard bands.
example: Four calls occupy 0-4 kHz, 4-8 kHz, 8-12 kHz, and 12-16 kHz on one copper pair at the same time.
scenario: Four calls use 0-4 kHz, 4-8 kHz, 8-12 kHz, and 12-16 kHz simultaneously on one pair. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: Simultaneous signals kept in separate frequency bands use frequency-division multiplexing.

definition: Multiplexing that gives each signal the full bandwidth during its own repeating time slot.
wrongs: Multiplexing that gives each signal a permanent frequency band.
Multiplexing that separates users only by spreading codes.
Multiplexing that puts each signal on its own optical wavelength.
why: Only one signal uses the channel in a given slot, and the slots repeat in a fixed frame.
example: Each of 24 phone calls is given the line in turn inside an 8000-frame-per-second PCM frame.
scenario: Each call gets the whole cable for a fixed slot in rotation, with a frame every 125 microseconds. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: Fixed repeating time slots that each get the full bandwidth are time-division multiplexing.

definition: Time multiplexing that assigns slots on demand to sources that currently have data to send.
wrongs: Time multiplexing that gives every source a slot in a fixed rotation even when it is silent.
Frequency multiplexing that reserves a band for each source at all times.
Wavelength multiplexing on an optical fiber.
why: Idle sources do not consume slots, so the link is shared according to actual traffic rather than a fixed roster.
example: A concentrator gives the next outgoing slot to whichever terminal has a byte waiting.
scenario: Slots go only to terminals that have bytes waiting, not to silent terminals in a fixed order. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: On-demand slots for active sources are statistical time-division multiplexing.

definition: Optical multiplexing that sends several signals on one fiber at different wavelengths.
wrongs: Electrical multiplexing that assigns each call a baseband frequency band on copper.
Time multiplexing that rotates fixed slots among callers.
Code multiplexing that separates users by spreading sequences.
why: Each optical carrier has its own wavelength, so many lightwave channels share one fiber.
example: One fiber carries traffic at 1550.12 nm and at 1550.92 nm at the same time.
scenario: One fiber carries simultaneous channels at 1550.12 nm and 1550.92 nm. Which multiplexing method is this?
scenarioWhy: Separate wavelengths on one fiber are wavelength-division multiplexing.

definition: Multiple access in which users share time and frequency but are separated by distinct spreading codes.
wrongs: Multiple access that gives each user a private frequency band.
Multiple access that gives each user a private repeating time slot.
Multiple access that gives each user a private optical wavelength.
why: Each transmitter multiplies its data by a code, and a receiver that uses the matching code extracts that user.
example: Two phones transmit together in the same band, and each base-station correlator keeps only its assigned code.
scenario: Users transmit together in the same band, and each receiver separates them with a unique code. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: Separation by spreading codes, while sharing time and frequency, is CDMA.

definition: Mapping a bit sequence onto a digital baseband waveform of voltage or optical pulses.
wrongs: Shifting bits onto a radio-frequency carrier by changing phase or amplitude.
Appending a polynomial remainder for error detection.
Compressing speech before uniform quantization.
why: Line coding chooses the pulse shape and the rules, such as NRZ or Manchester, used on a baseband line.
example: A serial link turns the bits 1011 into a sequence of +V and -V pulses before they enter the cable.
scenario: Bits are turned into voltage pulses on copper before any radio carrier is applied. Which mapping is this?
scenarioWhy: Mapping bits to a baseband pulse waveform is line coding.

definition: A line code that places a transition in the middle of every bit period so the receiver can recover the clock.
wrongs: A line code that holds one voltage level for the whole bit and can stay constant for long runs.
A bipolar code that uses a pulse only for 1s and sends zero voltage for 0s.
A passband method that encodes two bits in each carrier phase.
why: The guaranteed mid-bit transition removes long constant levels and provides a timing reference.
example: An IEEE 802.3 segment encodes every bit with a mid-bit transition so the NIC can stay synchronized.
scenario: Every bit period contains a mid-bit transition, and the receiver uses it to stay in sync. Which line code is this?
scenarioWhy: A transition in the middle of every bit period is Manchester encoding.

definition: Distortion in which energy from one symbol spills into adjacent symbol intervals at the sampling instant.
wrongs: Additive noise that is independent of the transmitted symbols.
The rounding error between a sample and its quantization level.
A parity failure caused by two flipped bits.
why: Band limiting spreads each pulse, so the receiver can sample a mix of the current symbol and its neighbors.
example: After a narrow channel, the sampler reads leftover voltage from the previous pulse added to the current one.
scenario: At the decision instant the receiver sees leftover voltage from the previous pulse added to the current pulse. Which impairment is this?
scenarioWhy: Symbol energy spilling into neighboring symbol intervals is intersymbol interference.
